passages.happening:
At Iconium, Paul and Barnabas go “as usual into the Jewish synagogue”, and they speak so well “that a great number of Jews and Greeks believed” (verse 1). “But the unbelieving Jews stirred up the Gentiles and poisoned their minds against the brothers” (verse 2).

Paul and Barnabas stay a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord, who confirms his message of grace with signs and wonders (verse 3). The city is divided. Some side with the Jews, and some with the apostles (verse 4).

When Gentiles and Jews, with their rulers, set out to mistreat and stone them, they learn of it and flee to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and the region around, where they go on preaching the good news (verses 5-7).
passages.hearers:
Iconium is the modern city of Konya, in central Turkey. Like Pisidian Antioch, it lay in the Roman province of Galatia.

Notice the first two words of verse 1: ‘as usual’. After ‘we now turn to the Gentiles’ in Pisidian Antioch (13:46), Paul goes straight back to the synagogue in the next town. That turn was for one town, not a turn away from the Jewish people. And here ‘a great number of Jews and Greeks believed’.

Then Luke writes of ‘the unbelieving Jews’. This time he says it plainly: the opponents are those Jews in Iconium who did not believe, set against the great number of Jews in the same town who did. When verse 4 says some ‘sided with the Jews’, it means this group of opponents, not the Jewish people. And verse 5 names Gentiles and Jews and the city's rulers together. Opposition came from more than one side. The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how verses like these were later misused against Jewish people, and why this site rejects that reading.

Luke calls Paul and Barnabas ‘apostles’ in verse 4 and again in verse 14. The word means ‘ones who are sent’. Here it seems to mean that the church at Antioch had sent them (13:3), a wider use than ‘the Twelve’.

They stay ‘a long time’, and they leave only when the danger is real. Fleeing a plot to kill them is not cowardice. Jesus had told his disciples, when persecuted in one town, to go on to the next (Matthew 10:23).
passages.ot:
‘Signs and wonders’ is an Old Testament phrase, used first of what God did in Egypt: God brought Israel out “with signs and wonders” (Deuteronomy 26:8). In Acts the same God confirms the message of his grace in the same way.

A divided city is an old picture too. The prophets were often welcomed by some and rejected by others in the same place. Jesus said his coming would bring division even within families (Luke 12:51-53), drawing on the prophet Micah (Micah 7:6).
passages.asks: Paul and Barnabas were driven out of one town and went on preaching in the next. Ask how you respond when people reject what you say about your faith. And notice ‘as usual’. Paul did not let one hard experience change how he treated the next group of Jewish people he met.

passages.happening:
In Lystra there sits a man crippled in his feet, lame from birth, who has never walked (verse 8). He listens to Paul. Paul looks straight at him, sees that he has faith to be healed, and calls out, “Stand up on your feet!” The man jumps up and begins to walk (verses 9-10).

When the crowds see it, they shout in the Lycaonian language, “The gods have come down to us in human form!” (verse 11). They call Barnabas Zeus, and Paul Hermes, “because he was the chief speaker” (verse 12).

The priest of Zeus, whose temple is just outside the city, brings bulls and wreaths to the city gates. He means to offer sacrifice with the crowds (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Lystra was a small city in the region of Lycaonia. Under the emperor Augustus it had been made a Roman colony, but its ordinary people still spoke their own Lycaonian language. That may be why Paul and Barnabas, who spoke Greek, do not realise at first what the crowd is shouting (verse 14).

No synagogue is mentioned here. For the first time in Acts, Paul preaches to people who do not know Israel's Scriptures at all.

The healing echoes Peter's healing of the man ‘lame from birth’ at the temple gate (3:2). Luke likes to show that Paul's work matches Peter's.

Zeus was the king of the Greek gods. Hermes was the messenger of the gods, so the man who did the talking was Hermes. Barnabas, perhaps the older or more dignified, was Zeus.

Why would people jump so fast to the idea that gods had come? The Roman poet Ovid, writing in the time of the emperor Augustus, tells an old story set in the hills of Phrygia, not far from here. Jupiter and Mercury (the Roman names for Zeus and Hermes) came to a town disguised as travellers. Everyone turned them away except one poor old couple, Baucis and Philemon, who welcomed them; the couple were rewarded, and the rest were punished. Scholars debate how far that story lies behind this scene. But if the people of Lystra knew such a tale, they would not want to miss the gods a second time.

The bulls were for sacrifice. The wreaths were garlands, often placed on the animals before they were killed. The whole town is about to worship two Jewish missionaries.
passages.ot:
The healing fulfils Isaiah's picture of God's coming: “Then the lame will leap like a deer” (Isaiah 35:6). Here the man ‘jumped up and began to walk’.

The Scriptures mock gods made by human hands. Their idols “have feet, but cannot walk” (Psalm 115:7). In Lystra a man who could never walk is healed by the living God, and the crowd thanks the idols.

The Old Testament also tells of heavenly visitors who came as travellers: the three men who came to Abraham's tent (Genesis 18:2). Abraham welcomed them, and Lot welcomed the two who went on to Sodom (Genesis 19:1-3). A story of gods in disguise, welcomed or turned away, was known in Israel too, but it led Israel to worship the one God, not to sacrifice to his messengers.
passages.asks: The people of Lystra saw something real and drew the wrong conclusion. Ask whether you ever give the credit for God's gifts to the wrong place: to a leader, to luck, to yourself. And notice the man who was healed: he had been ‘listening to the words of Paul’. Faith came from hearing before anything happened to his feet.

passages.happening:
When Barnabas and Paul find out, they tear their clothes and rush into the crowd, shouting, “Men, why are you doing this? We too are only men, human like you” (verses 14-15). They have come with good news, that the people should turn from these worthless things “to the living God, who made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them” (verse 15).

“In past generations, He let all nations go their own way” (verse 16). “Yet He has not left Himself without testimony to His goodness: He gives you rain from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling your hearts with food and gladness” (verse 17).

Even with these words, they can hardly stop the crowds from sacrificing to them (verse 18).
passages.hearers:
Tearing one's clothes was a Jewish sign of grief or horror, often at something said or done against God. Paul and Barnabas are appalled. Glory that belongs to God is being given to them.

Then comes the first speech in Acts to people with no Bible. Paul does not quote Scripture, because his hearers do not know it. He starts with what they do know: rain, harvests, food, gladness. Those good things, he says, are God's witness to them. The God who sends rain is not one of many gods. He is ‘the living God’, who made everything.

‘Worthless things’ means the idols and the sacrifices. That is a hard word, but Paul says it while refusing to be worshipped himself. He is not trying to win. He is pointing away from himself.

‘He let all nations go their own way.’ Paul does not say the nations were innocent. But he speaks of God's patience, not his anger. God was kind to them even when they did not know him, and now he calls them to turn.

What about people who lived and died without hearing of the living God? Paul does not answer that here, and Christians answer it in different ways. The Honest Answer ‘What about those who never heard?’ sets out the views.
passages.ot:
Paul's words come straight from Israel's Scriptures, even though he does not quote them by name. God is “the Maker of heaven and earth, the sea, and everything in them” (Psalm 146:6), as the commandments say: “in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth and the sea and all that is in them” (Exodus 20:11).

The God who sends rain is the God of the prophets: “the LORD our God, who gives the rains, both autumn and spring, in season” (Jeremiah 5:24). And ‘the living God’ is how the prophets set God apart from idols: “But the LORD is the true God; He is the living God and eternal King” (Jeremiah 10:10). Isaiah said, “All makers of idols are nothing, and the things they treasure are worthless” (Isaiah 44:9).
passages.asks: Paul met people where they were: in their fields, at their harvest tables. Ask how you would speak about God to someone who has never opened a Bible. Where in their ordinary life is God already giving ‘testimony to His goodness’? And notice how Paul and Barnabas refused praise. The surest sign of a true messenger is that he points away from himself.

passages.happening:
Then some Jews arrive from Antioch and Iconium and win over the crowds. They stone Paul and drag him outside the city, thinking he is dead (verse 19).

But after the disciples gather around him, he gets up and goes back into the city. The next day he leaves with Barnabas for Derbe (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
Again Luke says ‘some Jews’, and he tells us exactly who: opponents from Pisidian Antioch and Iconium, the same groups that had driven Paul out of those towns, who followed him a long way to Lystra. They are not the Jewish people. Paul, the man they stone, is himself a Jew, and in the towns they came from many Jews had believed (13:43; 14:1). The note on Acts 2:22-28 explains how such verses were later misused, and why this site rejects that reading.

The same crowd that wanted to worship Paul one day now stones him. Crowds are fickle.

Stoning was a way of killing by throwing large stones. Here it is mob violence, not a court's sentence. They drag him out of the city and leave him for dead. Paul later wrote, “once I was stoned” (2 Corinthians 11:25). He also remembered “the sufferings that came upon me in Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra” (2 Timothy 3:11).

Then the disciples gather around him. There are believers in Lystra now. Perhaps they were praying; Luke does not say. Paul gets up, walks back into the very city that stoned him, and leaves the next day for Derbe.

Paul once watched Stephen being stoned and approved (8:1). Now he knows what it is to be stoned for Jesus.

Paul's later helper Timothy came from Lystra (16:1-2). Paul wrote to him that Timothy had seen his sufferings there (2 Timothy 3:10-11). He may have been among the disciples standing around Paul that day.
passages.ot:
The Psalms are honest about the suffering of the faithful: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all” (Psalm 34:19). Paul, writing of these very towns, said the same: “What persecutions I endured! Yet the Lord rescued me from all of them” (2 Timothy 3:11).

Israel's prophets were stoned too. Zechariah son of Jehoiada was stoned in the temple court for speaking God's word (2 Chronicles 24:20-21). Paul stands in a long line of messengers who were hurt for what they said.
passages.asks: Paul got up and walked back into the city that had stoned him. Ask what it would take for you to go back to a place where you were hurt, if God asked it. And notice who stood around him: a small group of new believers. When someone falls, the church gathers round.

passages.happening:
In Derbe they preach the good news and make many disciples. Then they go back through Lystra, Iconium and Pisidian Antioch (verse 21), “strengthening the souls of the disciples and encouraging them to continue in the faith” (verse 22). “We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God,” they say.

Paul and Barnabas appoint elders for them in each church, praying and fasting as they entrust them to the Lord in whom they had believed (verse 23).

They pass through Pisidia and Pamphylia, speak the word in Perga, and go down to Attalia (verses 24-25). From there they sail back to Antioch, where they had been entrusted to the grace of God for the work they have now completed (verse 26).

When they arrive, they gather the church and report all that God has done through them, “and how He had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles” (verse 27). They stay there a long time with the disciples (verse 28).
passages.hearers:
Derbe was the furthest point of the trip. Beyond the mountains to the south-east lay Paul's home city of Tarsus, and the road on toward Syria. They could have gone home that way. Instead Paul and Barnabas turn round and go back through the very towns where they had been attacked. The new believers need them.

Their message to the young churches is honest: ‘We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God.’ They do not promise an easy life. They had just been stoned and chased out of town. Faith, they say, will cost something, and the kingdom is worth it.

Then they appoint ‘elders’ in each church: leaders to care for the believers after the missionaries leave. The Greek word for ‘appoint’ first meant to choose by a show of hands, and some read it to mean the churches had a say; by this time it often meant simply ‘appoint’. Elsewhere the New Testament calls such leaders shepherds and overseers (20:28; 1 Peter 5:1-2).

Churches today are led in different ways, and each finds roots in passages like this one. Some are led by bishops with priests or pastors under them, as in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican churches. Some are led by a group of elders together, as in Presbyterian churches. Some are governed by the members of each congregation, who choose their own leaders, as in Baptist and many other churches. These notes do not choose between them. All of them take from this verse that a church needs faithful leaders, chosen with prayer, and entrusted to the Lord.

They go home to Antioch and tell what God has done. Notice who did it: ‘all that God had done through them’. The trip was not their success. It was God's work, and the result was an open door for the Gentiles.

This trip took in the towns of the Roman province of Galatia. Many scholars think these are the churches Paul wrote to in his Letter to the Galatians. Others think that letter went to people farther north in the same province. These notes leave the question open.
passages.ot:
Appointing elders goes back to Moses. When the work grew too heavy for one man, God said, “Bring Me seventy of the elders of Israel known to you as leaders and officers of the people” (Numbers 11:16). Jethro had advised Moses to choose “capable men from among the people” and set them as leaders (Exodus 18:21). The church takes up the same wisdom: leadership shared, and entrusted to God.

‘Through many hardships’ has the shape of the Psalms and the prophets: “Many are the afflictions of the righteous, but the LORD delivers him from them all” (Psalm 34:19). And the ‘door of faith’ to the Gentiles opens on the promise Isaiah made to the servant of the LORD, to be “a light for the nations” (Isaiah 49:6).
passages.hard:
‘We must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God.’ Some people hear this as a promise of suffering, and they ask whether God wants his people to suffer.

The words do not say that suffering is good, or that it earns a place in God's kingdom. They say that following Jesus in a world that resists him will bring hard things, as it did for Jesus: “In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!” (John 16:33). Paul wrote of being “struck down, but not destroyed” (2 Corinthians 4:9).

Not every hardship comes from following Jesus, and not every hardship is meant to be endured in silence. If you are carrying something heavy, whether persecution, illness, loss, or harm at the hands of others, it is right to seek help and safety. Please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a counsellor. If you are in danger, or the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul and Barnabas went back through the towns where they had been hurt, to strengthen people who were just beginning. Ask who in your life is new in faith and needs someone to come back and check on them. And take their honest words with you: the way is hard, the kingdom is real, and the door is open.
